readings.c1s1:
¶
'''unworship†''' (un-wėr′ship), ''v. t.'' [ME., < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''worship.''] To dishonor; treat with dishonor. ''Wyclif'', Rom. ii. 23.

'''unworshiped, unworshipped''' (un-wėr′shipt), ''a.'' Not worshiped; not adored. ''Milton'', P. L., v. 670.

'''unworshipful''' (un-wėr′ship-fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unworshipful;'' < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''worshipful.''] Not entitled to respect; dishonorable.
{{smaller block|The ''unworshipful'' setes of dignitees.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, iii. meter 4.}}}}

'''unworth†''' (un-wėrth′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unworth, unwurth, onworth,'' < AS. ''unweorth,'' not worth, unworthy; as ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''worth''<sup>2</sup>.] Unworthy; little worth. ''Milton'', Tetrachordon.

'''unworth''' (un-wėrth′), ''n.'' Unworthiness. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Those superstitious blockheads of the twelfth century had reverence for Worth, abhorrence of ''Unworth.''
{{right|''Carlyle'', Past and Present, ii. 9.}}}}

'''unworthily''' (un-wėr′ᴛ̵ʜi-li), ''adv.'' In an unworthy manner; not according to desert; either above or below merit: as, to treat a man ''unworthily;'' to advance a person ''unworthily.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Lest my jealous aim might err
And so ''unworthily'' disgrace the man.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iii. 1. 29.}}}}

'''unworthiness''' (un-wėr′ᴛ̵ʜi-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unworthy; want of worth or merit.
{{smaller block|<poem>If thy ''unworthiness'' raised love in me,
More worthy I to be beloved of thee.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, cl.}}}}
readings.c1s3:
{{smaller block|<poem>His right arm ’s only shot,
And that compell’d him to forsake his sword;
He ’s else ''unwounded.''</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Malta, iv. 4.}}}}
'''2.''' Not hurt; not offended: as, ''unwounded'' ears.
{{smaller block|<poem>She, who can love a sister’s charms, or hear
Sighs for a daughter with ''unwounded'' ear.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Moral Essays, ii. 260.}}}}

'''unwrap''' (un-rap′), ''v.'' [< ME. ''unwrappen''; < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''wrap.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To open or undo, as what is wrapped or folded; disclose; reveal.
{{smaller block|Verray need ''unwrappeth'' al thy wounde hid.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Man of Law’s Tale, l. 5.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become opened or undone. ''Electric Rev.'' (Amer.), XV. xvii. 14.

'''unwrast†, unwrest†,''' ''a.'' [ME., < AS. ''unwrǣst'', infirm, weak, bad, < ''un-'', not, + ''wrǣst'', strong, firm.] Infirm; unreliable.
{{smaller block|He were ''vnwrast'' of hus worde that witnesse is of trewthe.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xxi. 313.}}}}

'''unwray†,''' ''v. t.'' A variant of ''unwry.'' ''North'', tr. of Plutarch, p. 25. (''Nares.'')

'''unwreaked''' (un-rēkt′), ''a.'' Not wreaked; unavenged; unrevenged. ''Spenser'', F. Q., III. xi. 9.

'''unwreath, unwreathe''' (un-rēth′, un-rēᴛ̵ʜ′), ''v. t.'' To undo, as anything wreathed; untwine; untwist. ''Boyle.''

'''unwrecked''' (un-rekt′), ''a.'' Not wrecked; not ruined; not destroyed. ''Drayton'', Upon Lady Aston’s Departure for Spain.

'''unwrest†,''' ''a.'' See ''unwrast.''

'''unwrinkle''' (un-ring′kl), ''v. t.'' To reduce from a wrinkled state; smooth.

'''unworthy''' (un-wėr′ᴛ̵ʜi), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ME. ''unworthy, unwurthy, onwurthy''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''worthy''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Not deserving; not worthy; undeserving: usually followed by ''of''.
{{smaller block|The most ''unworthy of'' her you call Rosalind.
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, iv. 1. 197.}}
None but those who are ''unworthy'' protection condescend to solicit it. {{right|''Goldsmith'', Vicar, xx.}}}}
'''2.''' Wanting merit; worthless; vile; base.
{{smaller block|Look you, now, how ''unworthy'' a thing you make of me!
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 2. 379.}}}}
'''3.''' Unbecoming; shameful; discreditable.
{{smaller block|<poem>The brutal action roused his manly mind.
Moved with ''unworthy'' usage of the maid,
He, though unarmed, resolved to give her aid.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Theodore and Honoria, l. 127.}}}}
'''4.''' Not having suitable qualities or value; unsuitable; unbecoming; beneath the character of: with ''of''.
{{smaller block|Something ''unworthy of'' the author. {{right|''Swift.''}}
I will take care to suppress things ''unworthy of'' him.
{{right|''Pope'', Letter to Swift.}}}}
'''5†.''' Not deserved; not justified.
{{smaller block|<poem>Worthy vengeance on thyself,
Which didst ''unworthy'' slaughter upon others.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., i. 2. 88.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' One who is unworthy. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester (1647-1680), born in Oxfordshire in 1647, was one of the ''unworthies'' of the reign of the “merry monarch, scandalous and poor.”
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XX. 614.}}}}

'''unwot†.''' See ''unwit.''

'''unwounded''' (un-wön′ded), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not wounded; not hurt; not injured by external violence. {{smaller block|<poem>His right arm ’s only shot,
And that compell’d him to forsake his sword;
He ’s else ''unwounded.''</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Malta, iv. 4.}}}}
'''2.''' Not hurt; not offended: as, ''unwounded'' ears.
{{smaller block|<poem>She, who can love a sister’s charms, or hear
Sighs for a daughter with ''unwounded'' ear.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Moral Essays, ii. 260.}}}}

'''unwreaked''' (un-rēkt′), ''a.'' Not wreaked; unavenged; unrevenged. ''Spenser'', F. Q., III. xi. 9.

'''unwreath, unwreathe''' (un-rēth′, un-rēᴛ̵ʜ′), ''v. t.'' To undo, as anything wreathed; untwine; untwist. ''Boyle.''

'''unwrecked''' (un-rekt′), ''a.'' Not wrecked; not ruined; not destroyed. ''Drayton'', Upon Lady Aston’s Departure for Spain.

'''unwrest†,''' ''a.'' See ''unwrast.''

'''unwrinkled''' (un-ring′kld), ''a.'' Not wrinkled; not having wrinkles or furrows; smooth; hence, flowing; even. ''Byron'', Childe Harold, iv.

'''unwrite''' (un-rīt′), ''v. t.'' To cancel, as that which is written; erase. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Yee write them in your closets, and ''unwrite'' them in your Courts.
{{right|''Milton'', Animadversions.}}}}

'''unwriting''' (un-rī′ting), ''a.'' Not writing; not assuming the character of an author. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The honest ''unwriting'' subject.
{{right|''Arbuthnot.''}}}}

'''unwritten''' (un-rit′n), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not written; not reduced to writing; oral; traditional: as, ''unwritten'' laws; ''unwritten'' customs.
{{smaller block|<poem>Predestinat thei prechen prechours that this shewen,
Or prechen inparfit ypult out of grace,
''Vnwryten'' for som wikkednesse as holy writ sheweth.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xii. 209.}}}}
{{smaller block|The proverbs themselves are no doubt often taken from that ''unwritten'' wisdom of the common people for which . . . Spain has always been more famous than any other country.
{{right|''Ticknor'', Span. Lit., I. 340.}}}}
'''2.''' Not written upon; blank; containing no writing.
{{smaller block|A rude, ''unwritten'' blank.
{{right|''South'', Sermons.}}}}
'''3.''' Not distinctly expressed, laid down, or formulated, but generally understood and acknowledged as binding: as, an ''unwritten'' rule; an ''unwritten'' constitution.{{smaller|—'''Unwritten law''', law which, although it may be reduced to writing, rests for its authority on custom or judicial decision, etc., as distinguished from law originating in written command, statute, or decree. See ''common law'', under ''common''.}}

'''unwrought''' (un-rât′), ''a.'' Not labored; not manufactured; not worked up.

{{smaller block|They [of Smyrna] export also a great deal of ''unwrought'' cotton. {{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. ii. 33.}}}}

'''unwrung''' (un-rung′), ''a.'' Not pinched; not galled.
{{smaller block|Let the galled jade wince, our withers are ''unwrung.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 2. 253.}}}}

'''unwry†''', ''v. t.'' To reveal; disclose. Also ''unwrie'', ''unwray.'' ''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 858.

'''unyielded''' (un-yēl′ded), ''a.'' Not having yielded; unyielding. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>O’erpowered at length they force him to the ground,
''Unyielded'' as he was, and to the pillar bound.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Pal. and Arc., iii. 651.}}}}

'''unyielding''' (un-yēl′ding), ''a.'' Not yielding to force, persuasion, or treatment; unbending; unpliant; stiff; firm; obstinate.
{{smaller block|With fearless courage and ''unyielding'' resolution.
{{right|''Edwards'', Works, III. 412.}}}}

'''unyieldingly''' (un-yēl′ding-li), ''adv.'' In an unyielding manner; firmly.

'''unyieldingness''' (un-yēl′ding-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unyielding; obstinacy; firmness. ''Daniel'', Hist. Eng., p. 47.

'''unyoke''' (un-yōk′), ''v.'' '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To loose from a yoke; free from a yoke.
{{smaller block|The chief himself ''unyokes'' the panting steeds.
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xxiii. 596.}}}}
{{smaller block|Her purple Swans, ''unyoak’d'', the Chariot leave,
{{right|''Congreve'', tr. of Ovid’s Art of Love.}}}}

'''2†.''' To part; disjoin.
{{smaller block|<poem>Shall these hands . . .
''Unyoke'' this seizure and this kind regret?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iii. 1. 241.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become loosed from, or as if

from, a yoke; give over work; hence, to cease.
{{smaller block|Ay, tell me that, and ''unyoke''. {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, v. 1. 59.}}
It is . . . but reason such an anger should ''unyoke'', and go to bed with the sun.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), I. 211.}}}}

'''unyoked''' (un-yōkt′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not having worn a yoke.—'''2†.''' Licentious; unrestrained.
{{smaller block|The ''unyoked'' humour of your idleness.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., i. 2. 220.}}}}

'''unyolden†''', ''a.'' [ME., < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''yolden'', pp. of ''yield''.] Same as ''unyielded''.
{{smaller block|<poem>By the force of twenty is he take
''Unyolden.''    ''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 1784.</poem>}}

'''unzealous''' (un-zel′us), ''a.'' Not zealous; destitute of fervor, ardor, or zeal. ''Milton'', Ans. to Eikon Basilike, § 9.

'''unzoned''' (un-zōnd′), ''a.'' Having no zone, belt, or girdle; ungirded; uncinctured.
{{smaller block|Full, though ''unzoned'', her bosom rose.
{{right|''Prior'', Solomon, ii.}}}}

'''up''' (up), ''adv.'' and ''prep.'' [< ''(a)'' ME. ''up'', ''upp'', rarely ''op'', adv. and prep., < AS. ''up'', ''upp'', adv., = OS. ''up'', ''upp'' = OFries. ''up'', ''op'' = D. ''op'' = MLG. LG. ''up'' = OHG. MHG. ''ūf'', G. ''auf'', adv. and prep., = Icel. Sw. ''upp'' = Dan. ''op'' = Goth. ''iup'', adv., up; ''(b)'' ME. ''uppe'', ''oppe'', ''ope'', < AS. ''uppe'' = MLG. ''uppe'' = Icel. ''uppi'', adv., up; Teut. *''up'', *''ūp'', perhaps connected with Goth. ''uf'', under, ''ufar'', over, = AS. ''ofer'' = E. ''over'': see ''over''. Cf. ''open''.]

'''I.''' ''adv.'' '''1.''' Of position or direction: In, toward, or to a more elevated position; higher, whether vertically, or in or by gradual ascent; aloft: as, to climb ''up'' to the top of a ladder; ''up'' in a tree.
{{smaller block|They presumed to go ''up'' unto the hill top.
{{right|Num. xiv. 44.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>True prayers
That shall be ''up'' at heaven and enter there
Ere sun-rise. {{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., ii. 2. 152.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller block|On the east and north side, at the top of the second story, there is a Greek inscription, but I had no conveniency of getting ''up'' to read it.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. i. 142.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>He heard a laugh full musical aloft;
When, looking ''up'', he saw her features bright.</poem>
{{right|''Keats'', Isabella.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And the souls mounting ''up'' to God
Went by her like thin flames.</poem>
{{right|''D. G. Rossetti'', Blessed Damozel.}}}}
{{smaller block|Specifically—(''a'') In or to an erect position or posture; upright: as, to sit or stand ''up''; to set chessmen ''up'' on the board; a stand-''up'' collar; in a specific use, on one’s feet: as, the member from A—— was ''up''—that is, was addressing the House.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Pelleas, leaping ''up'',
Ran thro’ the doors and vaulted on his horse.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Pelleas and Ettarre.}}}}
{{smaller block|(''b'') Above the horizon: as, the moon will be ''up'' by ten o’clock.}}
{{smaller block|And when the sun was ''up'' they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered away.
{{right|Mat. xiii. 6.}}}}
'''2.''' At or to a source, head, center, or point of importance: as, to follow a stream ''up'' to its source; to run the eye ''up'' toward the top of a page; to go ''up'' to London from Cornwall; often, in the direction of the north pole: as, ''up'' north: sometimes noting mere approach to or arrival at any point, and in colloquial or provincial use often redundant.
{{smaller block|<poem>When thai assent with syn of pride,
''vp'' for to trine my trone vnto.</poem>
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 8.}}
Send for him ''up''; take no excuse.
{{right|''Pope'', Imit. of Horace, II. vi. 36.}}
In his seventeenth year Oliver went ''up'' to Trinity College, Dublin, as a sizar. {{right|''Macaulay'', Goldsmith.}}
I was posting ''up'' to Paris from Bruxelles, following, I presume, the route that the allied army had pursued but a few weeks before. {{right|''J. S. Le Fanu'', Dragon Volant, i.}}
I’m Captain Joe Bell, out of a job. Seein’ your advertisement, I called ''up''. Where is the work, and what is it?
{{right|''The Century'', XXXIX. 225.}}}}
'''3.''' At, toward, or to a higher point or degree in an ascending scale, as of rank, quantity, or value: in many idiomatic and colloquial phrases. {{smaller|Noting specifically—(''a'') Rank, superiority, or importance: as, from a pauper ''up'' to a prince; to be ''up'' at the head of one’s class; to feel set ''up'' by success. (''b'') Extent, amount, or size: as, to swell ''up''; the death rate mounted ''up'' to fifty. (''c'') Price: as, stocks have gone ''up'' 3 per cent.; sugar has been ''up''. (''d'') Pitch, as of sound: as, this song goes ''up'' to A; to run ''up'' through the chromatic scale.}}
'''4.''' At, of, or to a height specified; of a particular measurement upward; as high as: usually with ''to'' or ''at''.
{{smaller block|I could tell you an excellent long history of my brother Ned’s envy, which was always ''up at'' high-water-mark.
{{right|''Walpole'', Letters, II. 150.}}}}

{{smaller block|The girls and women, too, that come to fetch water in jars, stand ''up to'' their knees in the water for a considerable time.
{{right|''Bruce'', Source of the Nile, I. 106.}}}}

'''5.''' At or to a point of equal advance, extent, or scope; abreast (of); so as not to fall short (of) or behind; not below, behind, or inferior (to): as, to catch ''up'' in a race; to keep ''up'' with the times; to live ''up'' to one’s income.

{{smaller block|We’ll draw all our arrows of revenge ''up'' to the head but we’ll hit her for her villany.
{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, iv. 2.}}}}

{{smaller block|The wisest men in all ages have lived ''up'' to the religion of their country.
{{right|''Addison.''}}}}

{{smaller block|They are determined to live ''up'' to the holy rule.
{{right|''Bp. Atterbury.''}}}}

{{smaller block|We must therefore, if we take account of the child-mind at all, interpret it ''up'' to the revelations of the man-mind.
{{right|''Science'', XVI. 351.}}}}

Hence—'''6.''' In a condition to understand, encounter, utilize, or do something; well equipped with experience, skill, or ability; equal (to): as, to be well ''up'' in mathematics; to be ''up'' to the needs of an emergency. [Colloq.]

<poem>The Saint made a pause
As uncertain, because
He knew Nick is pretty well ''up'' in the laws.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Barham'', Ingoldsby Legends, II. 199.}}}}

{{smaller block|It was not so well for a lawyer to be over-honest, else he might not be ''up'' to other people’s tricks.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Felix Holt, Int.}}}}

{{smaller block|“Come, Mercy, you are ''up'' to a climb, I am sure.” “I ought to be, after such a long rest.” “You may have forgotten how to climb,” said Alister.
{{right|''Geo. MacDonald'', What’s Mine’s Mine, p. 283.}}}}

{{smaller block|If an astronomer, observing the sun, were to record the fact that at the moment when a sun-spot began to shrink}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
